title: fork(): One Process Becomes Two
topic: fork() duplicates the calling process — both parent and child return from the same call with different return values, and run concurrently from there

beats.narration: What if a program could split itself in two — same code, same memory, but two living processes?

elements.content: what if a program could split itself in two?

beats.narration: Here is a process P. It has its own code, its own heap, its own stack — a private little universe with one thread of control.

elements.content: Process box with address-space stripes (stack, heap, data, code)
PC pointer marker on the code segment
one process: code, heap, stack, registers

beats.narration: Then P calls fork. The kernel makes an exact copy of the address space. Now there are two processes — a parent and a child — each with the same memory and registers.

elements.content: Parent process box on the left (PID 1234)
Child process box on the right (PID 1235), slides in from parent
Identical address-space contents in both boxes
exact copy — separate from this moment on

beats.narration: Both processes return from the very same call. The parent gets back the child's PID; the child gets back zero. That is how each one knows who it is.

elements.content: Branch arrow left, labelled rc = 0 → child
Branch arrow right, labelled rc > 0 → parent
fork() returns twice — and the value is the only clue

beats.narration: One call. Two returns. Two processes — running concurrently from there.

elements.content: One call. Two returns. Two processes.
(fork is the simplest way to spawn concurrent work)
